overview: Under Hafsid rule, Tunis was a wealthy center of the western Islamic world. Its urban history joins markets, religious institutions and residential neighborhoods. The surviving medina contains work from several dynasties, so individual buildings require their own dates and patronage histories.

items.text: Northern and southern suburbs developed in the thirteenth century around the older central medina. Tunis was an expanding urban settlement, not only a palace city.
Tunis connected the Maghreb, southern Europe and lands to the east. These links encouraged exchanges in architecture and the arts.
Souqs, residential quarters and gates formed an interconnected townscape. Their survival helps historians study urban organization alongside individual monuments.
Mosques and madrasas belonged to the city's institutional landscape. Surviving examples span both the Hafsid era and later periods.
Subsequent rulers added new palaces, residences and religious buildings. The medina records continuity and change across political transitions.
